current_example.title: Example: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain

q-129937.name: Question 1
q-129937.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[0,\pi ]\times [0,2].$
q-129937.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(\frac{1}{4+{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi }\cdot [\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{2})]_{0}^{2} \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{8}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

q-129937.html:
Question 1
?

Evaluate the double integral ∬Rsin⁡x4+y2dA over the rectangle R=[0,π]×[0,2].

a
 π2
b
 2π
c
 π
d
 π8
e
 π4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

∬Rsin⁡x4+y2dA=∬R(sin⁡x)(14+y2)dA=(∫0πsin⁡xdx)(∫0214+y2dy)=[−cos⁡x]0π⋅[12arctan⁡(y2)]02=−(cos⁡π−cos⁡0)⋅(12arctan⁡(1)−12arctan⁡(0))=−(−1−1)⋅(π8−0)=π4

q-71933.name: Question 2
q-71933.problem: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral ${∬}_{R}y\sqrt{xy}\text{ }\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,4]\times [0,1]?$
q-71933.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\sqrt{xy}\text{ }\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}y\,{x}^{1/2}\,{y}^{1/2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}({x}^{1/2})\text{ }({y}^{3/2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{y}\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

q-80507.name: Question 3
q-80507.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,e]\times [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
q-80507.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x})(\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{1}^{e}\cdot [\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

q-80510.name: Question 4
q-80510.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}{y}^{2}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2}]\times [0,3].$
q-80510.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}({csc}^{2}⁡x)({y}^{2})\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[-\operatorname{cot}⁡x]_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))\cdot (\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}) \\  & =(0+1)\cdot (9-0) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

q-129940.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,e]\times [e,{e}^{2}].$
q-129940.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x})\text{ }(\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{1}^{e}\cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{e}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡e) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

q-129955.name: Question 6
q-129955.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A=9+9=18.\end{aligned}
$$

q-71994.name: Question 7
q-71994.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-2){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{2}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[{y}^{3}]_{2}^{3} \\  & =(e-1)({3}^{3}-{2}^{3}) \\  & =19(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A=1-19(e-1)=20-19e.\end{aligned}
$$

q-80626.name: Question 8
q-80626.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A=2\,\text{Area}(R)=2\cdot (3\cdot 2)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =2({3}^{2}-(0)^{2}) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2y\,\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot [{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3({2}^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=12+18-24=6.\end{aligned}
$$

q-80642.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & =(8-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{8}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{8} \\  & =\frac{{8}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A=3+32=35.\end{aligned}
$$

q-81243.html:
Question 10
?

Evaluate the double integral ∬R3−4yx3ydA, where R=[1,2]×[1,e].

a
12−15e
b
15e−18
c
18e−15
d
15−12e
e
18−15e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

∬R3−4yx3ydA=∬R(3y−4x3)dA=∬R3y dA−∬R4x3 dA.

The function under the first integral is independent of x. So, we have

∬R3y dA=(2−1)∫1e3ydy=[3ln⁡|y|]1e=3ln⁡(e)−3ln⁡(1)=3.

The function under the second integral is independent of y. So, we have

∬R4x3 dA=(e−1)∫124x3dx=(e−1)[x4]12=(e−1)(24−14)=15(e−1).

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

∬R3−4yx3ydA=3−15(e−1)=18−15e.

q-81247.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $D$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{T}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={0,(x,y)∈S,cos⁡x+cos⁡y,(x,y)∈T,sin⁡xsin⁡y,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
∬Scos⁡ydA+∬Tcos⁡xdA+∬Usin⁡xsin⁡y dA
b
∬T(cos⁡x+cos⁡y)dA+∬Usin⁡xsin⁡y dA

∬S(cos⁡x+cos⁡y)dA+∬Tsin⁡xsin⁡y dA

∬Scos⁡xdA+∬Tcos⁡ydA+∬Usin⁡xsin⁡y dA
e
∬S(cos⁡x+cos⁡y)dA+∬Usin⁡xsin⁡y dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain D can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬S0dA+∬T(cos⁡x+cos⁡y)dA+∬Usin⁡xsin⁡y dA=∬T(cos⁡x+cos⁡y)dA+∬Usin⁡xsin⁡y dA.

q-130019.name: Question 12
q-130019.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=-3,\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=11,
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}\frac{1}{4}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$
q-130019.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}\frac{1}{4}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =\frac{1}{4}{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-3+11) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

q-130022.worked_solution:
First, notice that the domain $R$ can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =S\cup T\cup U.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{S}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{xy}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}0\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{xy}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Consider the region R shown above. Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={xy,(x,y)∈S,0,(x,y)∈T,x2+y2,(x,y)∈U. Then, ∬Rf(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬SxydA+∬T(x2+y2)dA
b
 ∬SxydA+∬U(x2+y2)dA
c
 ∬S∪Uxy(x2+y2)dA
d
 ∬SxydA+∬TdA+∬U(x2+y2)dA
e
 ∬S∪U(xy+x2+y2)dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the domain R can be represented as a union of three sub-domains, as follows:

R=S∪T∪U.

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬Sf(x,y)dA+∬Tf(x,y)dA+∬Uf(x,y)dA=∬SxydA+∬T0dA+∬U(x2+y2)dA=∬SxydA+∬U(x2+y2)dA.

a

q-80662.name: Question 17
q-80662.problem:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\, & \text{if}\,0<x<1,\,0<y<1, \\ {e}^{(x-y)},\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,0<y<1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{(0,2)\times (0,1)}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
q-80662.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =((0,1)\cup (1,2))\times (0,1) \\  & =((0,1)\times (0,1))\cup ((1,2)\times (0,1)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(0,1)\times (0,1)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (0,1)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(0,1)\times (0,1)}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (0,1)}{e}^{(x-y)}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
q-81251.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(-1,1)\times ((0,1)\cup (1,2)) \\  & =((-1,1)\times (0,1))\cup ((-1,1)\times (1,2)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(-1,1)\times (0,1)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(-1,1)\times (1,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(-1,1)\times (0,1)}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+y}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{(-1,1)\times (1,2)}x\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

q-81251.html:
Question 18
?

Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={x2+y,if−1<x<1,0<y<1,xln⁡y,if−1<x<1,1<y<2. Then, ∬(−1,1)×(0,2)f(x,y) dA=

a
∬(−1,1)×(0,1)x2+y dA+∬(−1,1)×(1,2)xln⁡ydA
b
∬(−1,1)x2+y dA+∬(0,1)xln⁡ydA
c
∬(0,1)x2+y dA+∬(−1,1)xln⁡ydA
d
∬(−1,1)×(0,2)x2+y dA+∬(−1,1)×(0,2)xln⁡ydA
e
∬(−1,0)×(0,2)x2+y dA+∬(0,1)×(0,2)xln⁡ydA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the rectangle R can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

R=(−1,1)×((0,1)∪(1,2))=((−1,1)×(0,1))∪((−1,1)×(1,2)).

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬(−1,1)×(0,1)f(x,y)dA+∬(−1,1)×(1,2)f(x,y)dA=∬(−1,1)×(0,1)x2+y dA+∬(−1,1)×(1,2)xln⁡ydA.
q-81251.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain

q-130044.name: Question 19
q-130044.problem:
Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A$, where

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}y{e}^{x+1},\, & \text{if}\,0<x<1,\,-2<y<0, \\ 3y\sqrt{x},\, & \text{if}\,1<x<4,\,-2<y<0,\end{aligned}
$$

and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$

q-130044.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain

q-130038.name: Question 20
q-130038.problem:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y+1}{1+{x}^{2}},\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,1<y<2, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}},\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,2<y<4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then,

$$
{∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,4)}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=
$$
q-130038.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =(1,2)\times ((1,2)\cup (2,4)) \\  & =((1,2)\times (1,2))\cup ((1,2)\times (2,4)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(1,2)\times (1,2)}\frac{y+1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,2)\times (2,4)}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130038.html:
Question 20
?

Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={y+11+x2,if1<x<2,1<y<2,x2y2,if1<x<2,2<y<4. Then, ∬(1,2)×(1,4)f(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬(1,2)×(1,4)(y+11+x2+x2y2)dA
b
 ∬(1,2)×(1,2)x2y2dA+∬(1,2)×(2,4)y+11+x2dA
c
 ∬(1,2)×(1,2)y+11+x2dA+∬(1,2)×(2,4)x2y2dA
d
 ∬(1,2)×(1,2)y+11+x2dA+∬(2,4)×(2,4)x2y2dA
e
 ∬(1,2)×(1,4)x2(y+1)y2(1+x2)dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the rectangle R can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

R=(1,2)×((1,2)∪(2,4))=((1,2)×(1,2))∪((1,2)×(2,4)).

So, we can write

∬Rf(x,y)dA=∬(1,2)×(1,2)f(x,y)dA+∬(1,2)×(2,4)f(x,y)dA=∬(1,2)×(1,2)y+11+x2dA+∬(1,2)×(2,4)x2y2dA.
